statement: In studies of pregnant women and their newborns published from 1982 to 2014 (24 articles from 19 studies, mostly cohorts; 15 of the 24 articles before 2000, editors' count; English only), any cannabis use during pregnancy as each study defined it (women using other illicit drugs left out, but not those who smoked tobacco or drank alcohol), compared with no cannabis use during pregnancy, is associated with somewhat smaller babies and more admissions to intensive care; whether it is linked to early birth is uncertain. In a 2016 meta-analysis whose pooled estimates are not stated to be adjusted for anything (the mean differences were pooled from raw group means, so they are unadjusted; Gunn et al., 2016; AMSTAR 2 critically low), exposed babies weighed on average about 109 g less at birth (95% CI 39 to 180 g; 10 studies, 4 of them finding lower weight; I2 63%), and had higher odds of weighing under 2,500 g (OR 1.77, 1.04 to 3.01; 7 studies, 2 of them positive; I2 89%) and of admission to neonatal or other intensive care (OR 2.02, 1.27 to 3.21; 4 studies, 3 positive; I2 78%); the estimate for preterm birth (before 37 weeks in most studies) fits both no difference and about twice the odds (OR 1.29, 0.80 to 2.08; 9 studies), and length of pregnancy, length and head size at birth, Apgar scores, birth defects and deaths around the time of birth showed no clear difference. No absolute risks were reported in the article, and the review does not discuss whether intensive-care admission reflects the babies' health or hospital practice toward babies of mothers known to use drugs (editors' observation). Mothers who used cannabis also had higher odds of anaemia (OR 1.36, 1.10 to 1.69; 6 studies), a result carried mainly by one large study. The review's authors say that, because most studies did not separate cannabis from tobacco and alcohol, and tobacco and heavy alcohol use are established causes of low birth weight, preterm birth and babies small for their gestational age, they cannot tell whether the associations come from cannabis. As described second-hand in narrative reviews and a professional statement: an earlier meta-analysis linked regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy with lower birth weight, a smaller reduction than with tobacco smoking, and one large study found no rise in birth defects (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009); later large studies reported that the lower birth weight generally persisted after statistical control for other drug use, although cigarette smoking has often been hard to adjust for fully, and self-reported use under-counts use, which Hall says probably weakens the associations (Hall, 2015); and in one US state with legal cannabis, prenatal use went with 1.5 times the odds of low birth weight after adjustment for maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use (OR 1.5, 1.1 to 2.1; Crume et al., 2018, as relayed by Page et al., 2020). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In studies mostly from before 2000, babies of women who used cannabis in pregnancy weighed on average about 109 grams less at birth than babies of women who did not, and more often went to newborn intensive care. Whether they were more often born early is not clear, and birth defects and deaths around birth were not clearly more common. Many of the mothers also smoked tobacco or drank alcohol; smoking and heavy drinking can also make babies smaller, and most studies did not separate them from cannabis, so the studies cannot show that cannabis caused the differences.
population: Pregnant women and their babies up to 6 weeks after birth, in 19 mostly cohort studies published from 1982 to 2014 in the USA, Canada, Australia, the Netherlands, Iran, Jamaica, Spain and Brazil; one later US state study as relayed by a professional statement
exposure: Any cannabis use during pregnancy as each study defined it (the authors note reliance on self-report, which may under-count use), with use of other illicit drugs excluded but tobacco and alcohol use allowed; frequency, amount, timing and potency not analysed
comparator: Women who did not use cannabis during pregnancy, and their babies (their tobacco and alcohol use not reported)
outcome: Birth weight; low birth weight (under 2,500 g); admission to neonatal or other intensive care; preterm birth (before 37 weeks); gestational age, length and head circumference; Apgar scores; birth defects and perinatal death; maternal anaemia
magnitude: Gunn et al. 2016 (pooled, no adjustment stated; random effects unless noted): birth weight about 109 g lower in exposed babies (printed as a positive mean difference, 109.42 g, 95% CI 38.72 to 180.12; 10 studies; I2 63%); low birth weight OR 1.77 (1.04 to 3.01; 7 studies; I2 89%); NICU or ICU admission OR 2.02 (1.27 to 3.21; 4 studies; I2 78%); preterm birth OR 1.29 (0.80 to 2.08; 9 studies; I2 85%); gestational age -0.20 weeks (-0.62 to 0.22; 5 studies; fixed effect); length -0.10 cm (-0.65 to 0.45; 6 studies; I2 59%); head circumference -0.31 cm (-0.74 to 0.13; 6 studies; I2 97%); maternal anaemia OR 1.36 (1.10 to 1.69; 6 studies; fixed effect). No absolute risks reported. As relayed by Page et al. 2020: one later US state study, low birth weight OR 1.5 (1.1 to 2.1) adjusted for maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use.

evidence.extracted: Seven databases searched from inception to 1 April 2014, English only. Eligible: women who used cannabis in pregnancy without other illicit drugs (cannabis groups that also smoked tobacco or drank alcohol were admitted), and their infants up to 6 weeks after birth (eligibility as recorded in the study card's sample section). 24 included articles from 19 unique studies by the authors' count (22 cohort, 1 case-control, 1 cross-sectional; no randomized trials), from the USA (10 articles), Canada (5), Australia (3), the Netherlands (2) and Iran, Jamaica, Spain and Brazil (1 each); published 1982 to 2014, 15 of the 24 before 2000 (editors' count from the reference list, on the study card).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs; Strengths and limitations of this study (box), 3rd to 5th bullets
evidence.extracted: The authors state that women who use cannabis often also smoke tobacco or drink alcohol and that most included studies did not exclude polysubstance use, so a cannabis-only effect could not be determined: it is unknown whether the associations relate to cannabis or to tobacco and alcohol use, tobacco and heavy alcohol use being, the authors say, established causes of low birth weight, preterm birth and small-for-gestational-age births. Few outcomes were measured or defined in a standard way, and reliance on self-report may have led to under-reporting of use.

evidence.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Reproductive effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (begins p. 1385, continues p. 1386); Conclusions, 1st paragraph (p. 1389)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: high doses of cannabis cause growth retardation and malformations in animals, but epidemiological studies give scarce evidence of birth defects, and the few associations are hard to interpret because women who use cannabis in pregnancy are also more likely to use tobacco, alcohol and other illicit drugs, less likely to seek antenatal care and more poorly nourished; one large study saw no increased risk of birth defects. Reduced birthweight is the most consistent association in large epidemiological studies, and a meta-analysis found that regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy decreased birthweight, though less than tobacco smoking did, which the authors attribute probably to carbon monoxide. Conclusion: use in pregnancy could reduce birthweight but does not seem to cause birth defects.

evidence.locator: Reproductive effects of cannabis use › Fetal development and birth defects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (begins p. 3, continues p. 4)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: birth defects were not consistently increased, the most convincing null result coming from a large study that measured use by urinalysis; a meta-analysis of studies from the 1980s and 1990s suggested that regular use in pregnancy reduced birth weight, less than tobacco smoking did; several later large studies reported that use in pregnancy is associated with reduced birth weight, an effect that has generally persisted after statistical control for other drug use, and some reported shorter labour and more babies small for gestational age. Limitations named: self-reported use is low and, by urinalysis studies, under-reported, which probably weakens the associations; and it has often been difficult to adjust fully for cigarette smoking.

evidence.page: pp. e14, e22 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Pregnant Women, 1st paragraph (p. e14); References, ref 70 (p. e22)
evidence.extracted: As relayed (Crume et al., 2018, ref 70): in a state with legal medical and recreational cannabis, self-reported use at any time in pregnancy was 5.7% (plus or minus 0.5%), and prenatal use was associated with low birth weight independently of maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use in pregnancy (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1 to 2.1; P = 0.02).

risk_of_bias.note: Pooled estimates not stated to be adjusted for anything (continuous outcomes pooled from raw means and SDs, so unadjusted; whether any odds ratio taken from a paper was adjusted is not said), in which tobacco and alcohol use, both known causes of low birth weight and early birth, are not separated from cannabis; exposure largely self-reported and under-reported; AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_gunn_2016). A stricter reading would rate down two levels; the floor is reached either way.

inconsistency.note: Unexplained heterogeneity in the significant pools (I2 63% to 89%); most single studies found no association (6 of 10 for birth weight, 5 of 7 for low birth weight).

indirectness.note: Worded for the exposure as studied (any use, in articles mostly published before 2000); the second-hand reports only qualify.

imprecision.note: Wide intervals for low birth weight (1.04 to 3.01) and intensive-care admission (1.27 to 3.21); the preterm interval (0.80 to 2.08) fits both no difference and a doubling, so the absence of a link is not shown; pooled numbers of participants are not reported.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; not downgraded separately.

large_effect.note: The intensive-care odds ratio (2.02) is not stated to be adjusted and is open to confounding by tobacco and alcohol; no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Residual confounding by tobacco and alcohol would more plausibly inflate than hide the associations; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low, the floor. Rated for the crude association as worded; these sources do not establish that cannabis causes the differences, and the review's authors say so. The narrative reviews and the professional statement are second-hand and overlap with the meta-analysis (Hayatbakhsh et al., 2012, is among its positive studies and among the later studies Hall, 2015, cites), so they qualify and are not counted as independent replication. Status mixed: the pooled estimates point to lower birth weight and more intensive-care admission, but most single studies found no association and the heterogeneity is unexplained.
